title: The five phases of the analytical lifecycle
text: The NHSBSA uses a five-phase analytical lifecycle to plan, produce, assure, communicate and review analysis. The lifecycle supports a consistent approach while ensuring lessons learned are carried forward into future work.

title: The five phases of the analytical lifecycle
text:
The lifecycle



The analytical lifecycle. Select the diagram to open it on its own page, where you can zoom in. Scroll sideways to see all of it.




Text description of this diagram


Five phases drawn as a circuit, read clockwise, each in a filled box with a line saying what happens in it. Phases 1, 2 and 3 run left to right across the top. An arrow comes down the right-hand side to Phase 4. An arrow runs back along the bottom to Phase 5. A dashed green arrow goes up the left-hand side from Phase 5 to Phase 1, closing the loop, and is marked: lessons go into the next scoping. Phase 5 is green and the other four are blue.

Phase 1, engagement and scoping. Define the requirement, intended use and impact of the analysis.
Phase 2, design. Select the most appropriate analytical approach and plan assurance activities.
Phase 3, analysis. Produce, document and assure the analysis.
Phase 4, delivery, communication and sign-off. Communicate findings, limitations and assurance outcomes.
Phase 5, review. Evaluate the effectiveness of the analysis and identify lessons learned.

section: Which standards apply to your work
text:
Which standards apply to your work
Two apply to everything NHSBSA produces, with no condition attached.

Standards that always apply, and what each does for you


Always
What it is, and what it does for you




GovS 010: Analysis
The government functional standard for analysis. Five principles, and three substantive requirements that the seven quality principles names. It sets the requirement


The AQuA Book
Good practice for analytical quality assurance: RIGOUR, the four roles, the four stages and proportionate assurance. It explains how to meet GovS 010 in practice



Then add whichever rows describe your work. More than one can apply at once.

Further standards by kind of work, and what each covers


Does this describe your work?
Then this applies as well
What it covers, and when it applies




It is official statistics
Code of Practice for Statistics, edition 3.0
In full, and as a regulatory requirement. Ten standards under Trustworthiness, Quality and Value. A narrower set of outputs than everything NHSBSA publishes


It involves code
NHSBSA Analytical Code Assurance Playbook
Version control, testing, peer review, readable and modular code, documentation, open sourcing. Whenever there is code


It is a Data Science initiative
NHSBSA Data Science Playbook
The end-to-end workflow: problem definition, assigning a critical friend, analysis, wrap up. It is the playbook that sequences your work


It produces a chart, table or dashboard
NHSBSA Data Visualisation Standards
How to choose a chart, how to label it and how to make it readable. In the Digital, Data and Technology Playbook


It is an open data release
NHSBSA Open Data Standards
How NHSBSA publishes open data


It is appraisal, or evaluation
Green Book, or Magenta Book
The Green Book for appraisal, covering the costs, benefits and risks of alternatives. The Magenta Book for evaluation, covering an intervention’s design, implementation and outcomes


You are assessing analytical risk
Orange Book
Risk management principles and concepts. Referenced by GovS 010 section 4.2


Data quality is a material concern
Government Data Quality Framework
Managing and describing data quality


It uses data or AI
Data and AI Ethics Framework
Seven principles. Its scope was extended to AI and algorithmic technologies in December 2025, so the principles cover both. See data ethics and personal data


A tool has a significant influence on a decision-making process with public effect, or directly interacts with the general public
Algorithmic Transparency Recording Standard
A record is required. An analytical model supporting broad policy-making sits outside that scope, and the assurance level does not decide it. Check at scoping. See algorithmic transparency and AI


It builds on or uses an AI system
AI Playbook for the UK Government, and Introduction to AI assurance from the Department for Science, Innovation and Technology (DSIT)
Ten principles for building, buying and using AI, and how a system is evaluated rather than just built


Any impact dimension scores 4
Business Critical, and Level 4 BCA
Business Critical analysis, in nine steps. This applies on top of everything above, and an AI system can still be Business Critical



Each one adds to the others. GovS 010 sets the requirement. The AQuA Book explains how to meet it. The Code of Practice adds obligations for official statistics. The code assurance playbook adds obligations where there is code. The Green, Magenta and Orange Books add depth for particular kinds of work. The AI guidance applies as well when a system, rather than an analysis, is being assured.
Where two appear to conflict, the more specific and more recent governs, and you should raise it. If this playbook disagrees with a standard, the standard is right and this playbook needs fixing. Who to ask has the route. You may also apply the Code of Practice voluntarily to work that is not official statistics, as a deliberate decision.
Every standard named here is linked from links to standards and guides.
What each standard asks for sets out what is in GovS 010, the AQuA Book and the Code of Practice for Statistics, and what RIGOUR means in full.

title: R7. Which standards apply to you
section: If your analysis uses AI or an algorithmic tool
text:
If your analysis uses AI or an algorithmic tool
This playbook does not cover building or assuring AI systems. These obligations apply when your analysis uses one.

The Data and AI Ethics Framework applies, in full. Its scope was extended to AI and algorithmic technologies in December 2025 and its seven principles cover both. Data ethics and personal data
The Algorithmic Transparency Recording Standard may apply, but its test is narrow. NHSBSA is in scope as an organisation, but within that the standard is mandatory only for tools with a significant influence on a decision-making process with public effect, or which directly interact with the public. An analytical model supporting broad policy-making is deliberately outside it. NHSBSA has two records on the public register, for the Prescriptions and Dental Exemption check and for the Residency Checker. These are the closest worked examples available. Algorithmic transparency and AI sets out the test, the two roles the standard names, and what this playbook proposes for NHSBSA.
The AI Playbook’s ten principles apply to the system, and DSIT’s assurance mechanisms are how it gets evaluated: risk assessment, algorithmic impact assessment, bias audit, compliance audit, conformity assessment and formal verification. Both are linked in links to standards and guides.
An AI system can still be Business Critical, and if it is, Business Critical analysis applies in addition to everything above.

Assure AI analysis the same way as any other analysis, and add the transparency duties above.

title: R5. Writing a quality assurance statement
text: A quality assurance statement tells a reader what was done to make the analysis trustworthy, and what its limits are. You need one at every level. Your level decides how much it carries and who sees it.
crumbs: R5. Writing a quality assurance statement

title: R5. Writing a quality assurance statement
text:
A worked example
This is a Level 2 Enhanced statement. Bracketed prompts show what belongs in each place.
It is illustrative, not approved wording. Use it to see what a statement contains and what each part is for, then write your own.

This analysis was produced by [analyst], [team], NHS Business Services Authority, in [month year] to support [the decision it informs].
It was assessed as Level 2 Enhanced on the NHSBSA Analytical Assurance Decision Tool. The basis was that it informs a directorate-level operational decision using linked internal data and an established statistical method.
Inputs were drawn from [source] as at [extract date]. [Named data quality issue] is present in the source and affects [which part of the result] by [scale or direction]. The method was independently reviewed by [reviewer] on [date], and the code is peer reviewed and version controlled at [repository].
Key assumptions and their sensitivity are recorded in the project record at [link]. The principal limitation is [limitation], which means these results should not be used to [the specific misuse this analysis cannot support].
Residual uncertainty is [description]. Questions about interpretation should go to [contact].

text:
What GovS 010 says about the statement
GovS 010 section 5.5 says the results should include an assurance statement. The statement covers assumptions, uncertainty, limitations, and comments on the applicability and use of the results.1
GovS 010 puts the statement as a should, not a shall. The playbook requires a statement at every level, and that requirement is the playbook’s own.

title: R3. Who to ask
text:
Communities of practice
Work with others from the start of the analysis. It gives you skills and knowledge from outside your team, avoids duplication, wasted effort and conflicting results, and brings wider professional perspectives.

Coffee and Coding
A monthly, hands-on session lasting 45 minutes to an hour, in which colleagues share a skill and everyone gets to run the code themselves. It has run since May 2021 and materials from every session are published at the Coffee and Coding page on GitHub.
Past sessions have covered R and Python from scratch, the Open Data Portal API, R Markdown and official statistics, accessible spreadsheets, and data visualisation. Anyone can attend, whatever their coding confidence, and you can take part without presenting.
For joining details, ask your team lead or the Data Science, Statistics and AI team.

title: R3. Who to ask
section: When the work needs a new skill
text:
When the work needs a new skill
Whoever assigns a piece of work has to give it to people with the skills, information and tools it requires. The person doing the work shares this responsibility equally.
There is no single analytical training catalogue to point you at. Follow these two steps.
Say so early. A skills gap found at scoping is a conversation about who else is involved, what training is needed, or whether the deadline moves. The same gap found at assurance is a finding against the analysis. Raise it with your team lead. If it is not resolved there, raise it with the Analytical Quality and Assurance Lead using the routes above.
Record it if it is not closed. Where the work goes ahead without the skill the assurance level assumes, that is a limitation of the analysis. Record it, and put it in the quality assurance statement, the same as any other limitation. See deciding your assurance level and Phase 4, delivery, communication and sign-off.

The quality assurance appraisal is one workbook of twelve worksheets. It includes the assumptions register and the risk and issue log, as the Scope template says. The worksheets are completed at three points in the life of the analysis.

Basic information is completed as document 6, as soon as the model has a name.
The analysis or model review is completed while the model is built and tested.
The assurance review is completed as document 10, by the critical friend as Lead Assurer, with the analyst.

The assurance review scores six areas: documentation, governance and oversight, structure and clarity, data and assumptions, verification, and validation. Outputs is a seventh area that NHSBSA has still to define.
Every requirement carries a reference code. The code links each action in the quality assurance plan to the criterion that raised it. For example, the Scope document is D1.
Business Critical analysis, step 5 asks for each action to be given a priority. The three priorities mean:

Must is essential to address a significant risk, issue or control weakness.
Should is recommended to improve quality, robustness or assurance.
Could gives additional benefit, but is not needed for the analysis to be acceptable.

The documentation held centrally by the Analytical Quality and Assurance function is the authoritative copy, and the function monitors Business Critical assurance activities. Analysts may keep working copies locally.
Naming each file with the document type first means the stack can be recognised at a glance, for example Scope_Specification_AnalysisName.
When a review raises a question about the method, go back to the technical guide, the Specification or the Scope. NHSBSA treats this as a normal part of maintaining a well-governed analysis.
Quality assurance continues after the analysis is judged fit for purpose, because data, methods, assumptions and requirements change. The actions are in Business Critical analysis, step 8.

title: R17. Why review, reuse and records matter
text:
Review and reuse

What a review looks at
These are the activities behind the questions in Phase 5, review.

Decisions taken and policy changes informed. Find what actually changed as a result of this analysis.
Usage. Check downloads, page views, requests, onward citation, or whatever else the publication route records.
Ongoing usefulness. Run user research with the people who use it, asking whether it still answers their question.
Case studies. Write down how the data has been used, as it happens.
Trend changes. Where the analysis was meant to change a trend, check whether the trend changed.
Improvements to regular analysis. Note what the last run of this analysis showed could be better.
Decommissioning. Stop producing analysis that is no longer useful.



Review activities and the standards behind them
The first four review activities above are how the playbook acts on Code of Practice Standards 8 and 9. The Code does not list them.
Standard 8 asks producers to review user satisfaction routinely.1 It also asks them to take views from a range of users on when statistics are started, stopped or changed.1 That is where decommissioning sits.
Standard 9 asks producers to explain how the statistics add value and how they could inform decision making.2
The Code applies in full to official statistics and is voluntary for other analysis. See applying the Code voluntarily and which standards apply to you.
GovS 010 section 6.10 covers improvements to regular analysis. It asks for lessons to be captured through the analytical cycle, evaluated and acted on.3
Checking whether a trend the analysis was meant to change actually changed is the playbook’s own. No standard asks for it.


The monthly review meeting
NHSBSA holds a review meeting every month for regular and ongoing outputs. The Analytical Quality and Assurance Lead chairs it. It checks that the output was peer reviewed, was completed correctly, and still answers the question it was built for. The owner of each regular or ongoing output brings it to the meeting.


Checking again after release
Data, methods and the question all change over time. AQuA Book section 5.3 says that where analysis is used on an ongoing basis, all aspects of the lifecycle should be regularly updated.4
Reuse tests the assumptions the original was built on. That is why reuse for a new purpose triggers a review at every level above the first.
Each of the four checks before reuse asks whether one of those assumptions still holds.

Population. The new use may be about a different population from the one the analysis covers.
Data. The data may have moved in coverage, definition or quality since.
Use case. The new use may be outside what the method was built to answer.
Decision context. The output may now carry more weight, so the same figure is relied on for more than it was.

A yes to any of the four means the work goes back to deciding your assurance level, where the level is scored again. If all four answers are no, the reuse goes ahead on the level the work already carries.


Reuse and the assurance level
Because reuse tests the assumptions the original was built on, a Business Critical designation is revalidated before any reuse for a new purpose.
Reuse is one legitimate reason to change a level or a score. That is the playbook’s own view, and no standard states it.
AQuA Book Table 3-1 lists reusing or repurposing existing work among the factors for determining appropriate assurance. It says reusing work may require validation and verification to confirm the original approach.5
GovS 010 section 6.11 says the senior accountable officer should approve the use of a recommended practice model for a purpose other than the one it was designed for, or where the context of its use has changed.6
Scoring again says when a scheduled output, or a one-off that becomes a production run, is scored again.


Capturing lessons, and what to raise wider
Lessons are captured as they happen, rather than reconstructed at the end. GovS 010 section 6.10 asks for them to be captured throughout the analytical cycle.3
Case studies are also written down as the data is used.
Lessons are recorded where the next analyst will look for them. For a regular output, that is the analytical plan for the next cycle.
Raise anything that applies beyond one output more widely. Examples are a method that did not work, a data quality problem, and an assurance step that was disproportionate in either direction. See who to ask for who to go to.


Peer review during the work, and review in Phase 5
Peer review and independent challenge happen during the work. They decide whether the output can be released. What the critical friend confirms lists what that review confirms. The checks themselves are in the checks, by level.
Two GovS 010 clauses apply. Section 6.6 covers verification and validation, which are conducted throughout the analytical cycle.7 Section 6.8 covers quality assurance, which includes peer review by independent individuals or groups.8
Phase 5 review is a different activity. It covers what happens to an output after release. It asks whether the output is still useful, and what the next piece of work should do differently.
GovS 010 section 6.10, on learning from experience, covers what the next piece of work should do differently.3

title: R17. Why review, reuse and records matter
text:
Records and logs

The quality assurance log and the checklist
A checklist shows somebody knew what to do. A log shows they did it, when, and what they found.
What your level requires asks for the log to record each check done, when it was done, what was found and the conclusion drawn. GovS 010 section 6.6 asks analysts to document verification and validation activities and the associated conclusion.7 The aim is that the utility and reliability of the analysis can be assessed afterwards.


Keeping the project record beside the output
Keep the project record beside the output, so anyone who finds the output can also find how it was made. GovS 010 section 6.7 says documentation, data and other records should be version controlled, securely stored as needed and retrievable if needed, to support and evidence analyses.9
At Level 1 the record is about one side of A4. Only the parts of the project record marked Yes for Level 1 are completed.


Logging decisions as they are made
A log written from memory at the end is a much weaker document. That judgement is the playbook’s own.
GovS 010 section 6.7 says record keeping and documentation can include notes of any deviations from the plan and a log of data and assumptions.9

title: R15. Why Business Critical works as it does
text:
Reaching the designation

What makes work Business Critical
NHSBSA’s definition of Business Critical analysis is on Business Critical analysis. A Level 4 score on any of the six impact dimensions of the Analytical Assurance Decision Tool identifies work as Business Critical.
One dimension at Level 4 is enough.
In this playbook, the designation is a consequence of the impact assessment, not a separate judgement alongside it. It comes from scoring the six impact dimensions on the Analytical Assurance Decision Tool, which sets the assurance level in any case.
In this playbook, nobody settles it separately or anywhere else. The Business Critical steps follow from the designation.
The Analytical Risk Assessment and Quality Assurance Framework lists escalation to Business Critical Analysis separately. It gives four triggers, joined by “and/or”:

a Very High risk rating
errors that could result in significant financial, legal, operational or reputational consequences
support for nationally significant or high-profile decisions
being part of a recognised Business Critical Model

None of the four designates work as Business Critical on its own. The framework says designation is a governance decision, to be considered separately from the analytical risk rating.
Where work was not designated at scoping, the playbook treats a trigger as a reason to score the six impact dimensions again with the commissioner.

Publication status and other signs of visibility
NHSBSA’s guidance says that none of these justifies a Level 4 score by itself:

publication status
Board consideration
Official Statistics designation
media interest
national visibility
Freedom of Information (FOI) disclosure
ministerial interest
parliamentary scrutiny

These things raise how much assurance the work needs. They do not, on their own, make the analysis Business Critical. The playbook scores them once, under public visibility and reach.
NHSBSA’s worked examples for impact are marked as still to be developed. They place a Board report, an FOI response and a ministerial briefing at impact 3, not impact 4.
Official statistics are assured under the Code of Practice for Statistics, which GovS 010 says producers of official statistics should apply,1 whether or not they are Business Critical. The two are different questions, and a publication answers both separately.



Settling the level at scoping

The impact is scored first
You decide whether work is Business Critical at scoping. The impact score alone settles it, which is why the impact comes first.
Everything that follows from a designation takes time to arrange: the register entry, the Analysis Senior Responsible Officer and the enhanced assurance. Revalidation later confirms that the designation still holds.


The tool is used when the Scope is complete
NHSBSA’s guidance names the time. It calls the tool the assurance decision sheet and says it “can be used when the scope is completed” (section 5.1).
The guidance allows the tool to be used then. The playbook requires it.
The Scope defines the key decisions the analysis supports and its principal risks. The six impact dimensions ask about the same things.
A designation reached after the Specification is written cannot change the Specification. If two analysts doing comparable work reach different levels, the reason should be recorded.
The commissioner knows what the analysis will be used for and what depends on it. The analyst knows what the analysis can support. That is why the two score together.


A Level 4 BCA level holds at every likelihood
Every cell in the impact 4 row of the matrix is Level 4 BCA. The row does not vary, so no likelihood score can move the level.
Where an impact dimension scores 4, your level is already Level 4 BCA at scoping. Nothing below impact Level 4 reaches Level 4 BCA, however likely an error is.


A full likelihood check is not required
The likelihood stays part of the Business Critical route, as step 3, read the assurance level shows. A full check of it in the Analytical Assurance Decision Tool is not required, because it cannot change the level.


The answer is recorded either way
The playbook asks for a no to be recorded as well as a yes.

title: R15. Why Business Critical works as it does
text:
After the designation

The register entry, for models and other analysis
Business Critical work is logged with the Data Science, Statistics and AI team on the Business Critical register. NHSBSA’s earlier guidance gave the register of analytical models to the Quality and Assurance team (NHSBSA Business Critical Analysis: Navigating the Assurance Journey, 17 September 2026). The playbook follows NHSBSA’s current arrangement. The playbook puts any Business Critical work on the register, whether or not it is a model, because analysis that is not a model can still be Business Critical.
In this playbook, a model is analysis built to be run more than once, usually over time. GovS 010 section 6.11 says what models used in decision making should be, and what recommended practice models should have.2 For a model, the requirements of the Business Critical steps apply across its whole life, not just to the run that produced today’s number.
GovS 010 section 6.11 does not mention a register. It says each recommended practice model should have five things, and they are the five items that the register entry holds.2 That is a should, which is a recommendation. The AQuA Book goes further at sign-off. It says the analyst and the approver shall follow organisational governance procedures, including updating the business-critical analysis register where appropriate.34 For Business Critical work, the playbook requires the entry.
In this playbook, Business Critical work is on the register and every entry on it has a review date. No standard states the review-date rule.


The public register and annual reporting
Each entry is added to NHSBSA’s public register of Business Critical analyses. NHSBSA reports on its Business Critical analysis every year to the Data, Analytics and AI Governance Council and to the Department of Health and Social Care, and includes a statement in its annual report.


Approving a new use
GovS 010 section 6.11 puts approval of a new use as a should, which is a recommendation. The senior accountable officer should approve a recommended practice model that is used for another purpose, or whose context of use has changed.2 In this playbook, that officer is the Analysis Senior Responsible Officer.
For Business Critical work, the playbook treats approval as a condition of staying on the register.
Reuse is also the usual reason an assurance level changes. Reuse and the assurance level explains why.


Quantifying uncertainty at Level 4 BCA
At Level 4 BCA, uncertainty is quantified wherever the method allows. That is the same as Level 3.
GovS 010 section 6.5 asks for expressions of uncertainty to be quantitative where possible when results are disseminated.5 Uncertainty, assumptions and limitations covers the method.


Revalidation of the designation, in both directions
A designation is not permanent. Work that was Business Critical can stop being so, and work that was not can become so as its use widens.
Revalidation therefore checks the designation in both directions. It is part of the Phase 5 review, not a separate exercise.

text: Where an algorithmic or AI tool is part of the analysis, three things follow. Publish what the tool does. Make sure a person can change the outcome. Be clear about any AI used to produce the work.

title: R11. Algorithmic transparency and AI
section: Check whether your tool needs a transparency record
text:
Check whether your tool needs a transparency record
There are two tests. Both must be met. Make the check at scoping and record the answer either way, because a record takes drafting and clearance.

Algorithmic transparency scope tests and where NHSBSA analysis lands






The test
Where NHSBSA analysis lands




Is the organisation in scope?
Yes. The standard is mandatory for arm’s length bodies which deliver public or frontline services, or directly interact with the general public. NHSBSA does both


Is the tool in scope?
Usually not. Mandatory only where the tool has a significant influence on a decision-making process with public effect, or directly interacts with the general public. An analytical model supporting broad policy-making is deliberately outside it

title: R11. Algorithmic transparency and AI
text:
Algorithmic transparency
The Algorithmic Transparency Recording Standard (ATRS) is how a public body publishes what an algorithmic tool does. The record says what the tool is for and what data it was built on. It also says how the tool affects decisions, who is accountable for it, and what oversight it has.
First test, the organisation. The standard is mandatory for all government departments. It is also mandatory for arm’s length bodies which deliver public or frontline services, or directly interact with the general public.1
NHSBSA does both, so the organisation is in scope. The standard is recommended across the rest of the public sector, which is not in mandatory scope.1
Second test, the tool. Within an organisation in scope, the standard is mandatory for algorithmic tools which have a significant influence on a decision-making process with public effect. It is also mandatory for tools which directly interact with the general public.1

Most of the analysis this playbook covers is outside the mandatory scope
The standard applies to tools “influencing specific operational decisions about individuals, organisations or groups”. It does not apply to “an analytical model supporting broad government policymaking”.1
An eligibility rule, a risk score or a triage tool applied to individual cases is an operational decision about individuals, so it is in scope. An analytical model that supports broad policymaking is not. The test is what the tool decides, and about whom. It is not how visible the analysis is, and it is not the assurance level it scored.
You can still publish a record for a tool outside the mandatory scope. The Data and AI Ethics Framework recommends publishing a record “even where a tool does not strictly fall within scope of the ATRS”.2
Ask whether the tool is in scope in the same conversation that scores the impact. A record takes drafting and internal clearance before it can be published, so allow time for that.


The transparency record and Business Critical status
The two decisions are separate. An analysis can be Level 4 BCA and still be out of ATRS scope. It can be Level 2 Enhanced and in it.
Being Business Critical does not by itself put a tool in the scope of the Algorithmic Transparency Recording Standard. Being outside that scope does not make the tool less critical. Each has its own test, and both tests are applied at scoping.


State in the output what the method does not show
Where a method cannot be explained, you must state that limitation in the output. A vendor-supplied scoring tool whose weighting is not disclosed is one example. If the tool is in ATRS scope, put the limitation in the record as well.
If a model’s internal workings cannot be inspected, assure it in the same way as any other model. The difficulty is in transparency, in having the right mix of experts available, and in understanding what mitigations are possible. It is not a reason to assure the model less.


Who drafts and publishes the record
The standard names two roles. An organisation in mandatory scope should have a named single point of contact for the standard, whose job is to coordinate with the standard’s own team on identifying the tools in scope, drafting the records and publishing them.
If you do not know who yours is, the guidance says to ask algorithmic-transparency@dsit.gov.uk.1 Each record names a senior responsible owner, given as a role title rather than a person. That role is ultimately accountable for the tool in an operational context.3
Who holds each of those at NHSBSA is a governance decision rather than something the standard settles, and neither is settled yet. Until they are, the analyst drafts the record as part of delivery. The Lead Official for Statistics clears it before publication, as for a published statistic.
That route is this playbook filling a gap rather than the standard requiring it. Check it with the analytical assurance mailbox in who to ask.

title: R11. Algorithmic transparency and AI
text:
Meaningful human oversight
“A human is involved” is not oversight on its own. It can be true when nobody is able to change the outcome.
Start with the law. UK General Data Protection Regulation (UK GDPR) article 22 prohibits decisions based solely on automated processing that have legal or similarly significant consequences for an individual. A service using an algorithmic tool that affects a person’s legal status or rights may use it only to support a human decision-maker’s decision.4
Where article 22 does not apply, how much human involvement is enough depends on three things. They are the complexity of the output, its potential impact, and how much specialist knowledge reading it requires.4 Design, document and assess the points where human review happens, and what further information the reviewer takes into account.4
Five questions make oversight real rather than nominal.

Questions on human oversight and what a usable answer looks like






Question
What a usable answer looks like




Who reviews the output?
A named role, not “the team”. Oversight with no named owner does not happen


What authority do they have?
Can they change the answer, or only note a concern about it


When can they challenge or override?
Before the decision is acted on, or only after somebody complains


What gets recorded?
That a review happened, what it considered, and what it changed


Can the decision be reviewed or appealed?
By the person it was about, and through what route



If the reviewer has no authority to change the answer, name a reviewer who has.

title: R11. Algorithmic transparency and AI
section: Using AI tools to do the analysis
text:
Using AI tools to do the analysis
This is different from analysis of an algorithmic tool. It is the everyday case: an analyst using an AI assistant to write code, summarise a document, draft a passage or explain an error.
Using an AI tool changes nothing about who is accountable for the output.

Ask before you use a tool that is not already in use in your team. NHSBSA has no published list of approved analytical AI tools, so the default is to ask rather than to assume.
Do not put data into a tool that is not cleared to hold it. Patient data, personal data and anything under a data sharing agreement are the obvious cases. Use a tool for such data only if someone with the authority has said yes in writing.
Verify what comes back. An AI output is a statistically informed guess rather than a fact.5 Test code, check a summary against its source, and recalculate a figure.
Accountability does not transfer. The analyst who signs the output owns everything in it. “The tool produced it” is not a finding, a caveat or a defence.
Record material use where it affects reproducibility. If someone repeating your work needs to know a tool was used to derive something, say so in the project record, and say what was checked.5 Spell-checking a paragraph is not material. Generating the transformation logic behind a published figure is.

title: R9. Uncertainty, assumptions and limitations
text:
What the terms mean, and how uncertainty is identified, quantified and communicated.
Phases 2 and 3. Phase 2, design and Phase 3, analysis.
All analysis is uncertain. Identify your uncertainty, manage it, and tell the reader about it in terms they can act on.

title: R9. Uncertainty, assumptions and limitations
text:
What uncertainty is
Uncertainty describes the difference between an estimate and the true value. It arises from measurement and sampling error, how data was collected, and missing data. It also arises from under-reporting, the assumptions you had to make, and the limits of the method itself.
Direct uncertainty is uncertainty about an estimate that can be measured or quantified. It is communicated in absolute terms: a standard error, a confidence or credible interval, statistical significance.
Indirect uncertainty is uncertainty about the underlying quality of knowledge surrounding an estimate. It is not directly measured but inferred from the analysis.
Indirect uncertainty is usually communicated as caveats. It can also be summarised on a qualitative or ordered scale such as the GRADE scale. The GRADE scale grades how much confidence to place in a body of evidence.
Most analysis has both. Report both, not only the one with a number attached.

Uncertainty in a forecasting model
State the uncertainty beside a forecast, because what the model does not know is most of what the reader needs. Communicating it sets out how to state it.

title: R9. Uncertainty, assumptions and limitations
text:
Plan for uncertainty at design
Address uncertainty during the analytical cycle. That lets you design and plan the analysis proportionately, and choose your assumptions, options and scenarios.1
At design, you can choose a method that reduces uncertainty. By the time you write up, you can only describe it.
At design, search the planned analysis systematically for sources and types of uncertainty.2 Look for any large enough to exceed the acceptable margin of error, so you can design for them. GovS 010 section 5.3 says the designed approach should consider uncertainty.3
You should:1

identify the sources of uncertainty and consider their impacts
analyse it at the level the decision requires, and no further
develop options for managing it, and take appropriate control and mitigation actions

title: R9. Uncertainty, assumptions and limitations
text:
Assumptions
An assumption is something you have taken to be true without establishing it. Every analysis has them. What matters is recording them.
For each material assumption, record:

The fields of an assumptions entry and what goes in each






Field
What goes in it




The assumption
Stated plainly, so someone else can judge it


Rationale
Why it is reasonable


Impact if wrong
The direction and rough scale of the error if the assumption fails


Sensitivity tested
Yes or no. Testing is first required at Level 2 Enhanced, where material


Agreed with
Who accepted it, and when



If an assumption failing would not change the conclusion, record it briefly. If it would reverse the conclusion, state it in the output itself.
Where you can, test the sensitivity of your key assumptions, and plan that testing in Phase 2, design, not after the analysis is done. You and the commissioner agree the acceptable margin of error at scoping, along with the levels of quality and certainty the analysis needs.4 Sensitivity testing shows whether an assumption could take the analysis past that margin.
Deciding your assurance level first requires sensitivity testing at Level 2 Enhanced, where it is material. Levels 3 and 4 inherit that requirement.

title: R9. Uncertainty, assumptions and limitations
text:
Limitations
A limitation is something your analysis cannot do. State them in terms of use, not method, because the reader is deciding how to use the analysis.
Instead of “the data has incomplete coverage for two months”, write “these figures understate activity in July and August, so they should not be used to compare quarters”.
Write a sentence that begins “this analysis should not be used to…”, and name the specific misuse it cannot support.

title: R9. Uncertainty, assumptions and limitations
text:
Communicating it
When you share results, expressions of uncertainty should:1

be quantitative where possible
be balanced, avoiding unwarranted confidence in a particular option

In practice:

Be transparent about uncertainty, to avoid misinterpretation and misuse
Be specific about what exactly is uncertain and why, how it has been quantified, the limitations of the data, and the assumptions made
Use plain language, so everyone who reads what you write about uncertainty can understand it
Show it in your visualisations, data tables and datasets, and explain what it represents. Put it in the main output, not only in a quality and methodology annex

For official statistics, Standard 7 of the Code of Practice requires producers to prominently explain quality, including strengths and limitations. It also requires them to communicate the uncertainty in estimates. See which standards apply to you.

title: Business Critical analysis
section: Step 1. Decide at scoping whether it is Business Critical
text:
Step 1. Decide at scoping whether it is Business Critical
Do this when the Scope is complete, before the Specification is written.

Score the six impact dimensions with your commissioner in the Analytical Assurance Decision Tool spreadsheet, which describes each dimension at each level. Score each from Level 1 to Level 4 and take the highest. Opening it needs an NHSBSA account with access to the Analytical Quality and Assurance site.
The work is Business Critical if any one dimension scores Level 4.
Keep Level 4 for a material consequence. The tool says: “Publication status, Board consideration, Official Statistics designation, media interest, national visibility, FOI disclosure, ministerial interest or parliamentary scrutiny do not by themselves justify a Level 4 score.” Score those under public visibility and reach.
If you and your commissioner disagree, escalate to the Analytical Quality and Assurance Lead.
Save the completed Analytical Assurance Decision Tool and append it to the quality assurance plan, as its template asks. Record the answer, yes or no.
Check whether the Algorithmic Transparency Recording Standard applies to any algorithmic tool in the work. It does if the tool:

has a significant influence on a decision-making process with public effect, or
interacts directly with the general public.

Record the answer either way. Algorithmic transparency and AI has the test.

text:
Step 2. Name who is accountable
The commissioner names an Analysis Senior Responsible Officer at scoping, with the Analytical Quality and Assurance Lead.

They must be senior enough to carry the risks across the lifecycle.
They approve the work as fit for purpose before it is used.
The commissioner may take the role.

section: Step 9. Review the work and revalidate the designation
text:
Step 9. Review the work and revalidate the designation
Revalidate the designation as part of the Phase 5 review. The Analysis Senior Responsible Officer does this annually, and before any reuse for a new purpose.
Check whether work that was Business Critical still is, and whether work that was not has become Business Critical as its use widened.
After sign-off, keep assuring the work:

Check that it is used as intended, with its caveats.
Log any errors and record any improvements.
Keep data and assumptions up to date through scheduled reviews.
After any material change, review the scope, the specification, the user and technical guides, and the quality assurance appraisal and plan, in proportion to the change.

title: How to contribute
text:
Submitting a pull request
Please submit new contributions via a pull request:

Fork or clone the repository
If you want to run the page on your machine, configure and install the dependencies. See the README for details.
Create a new branch: (e.g. git checkout -b my-branch-name)
Make your change
Push to your fork and submit a pull request

Your pull request will then be reviewed. You may receive some feedback and suggested changes before it can be approved and your pull request merged.

To increase the likelihood of your pull request being accepted:

If you are making visual changes, include a screenshot of what the affected element looks like, both before and after.  
Give every table a caption: a line that starts with : directly under the table, after a blank line. A first column of bold labels becomes row headers on its own.
Keep your change as focussed as possible. If there are multiple changes you would like to make that are not dependent upon each other, consider submitting them as separate pull requests.
Write good commit messages.

title: How to contribute
text:
Getting started with development

Environments

Github Codespaces
The easiest way is just to open the repo in Github Codespaces - you can then make your changes, run the website to check it, and commit those back all within a VSCode environment.


Working locally
If you don’t want to use Github codespaces (or can’t because it’s blocked, or you’ve run out of credits), then you can make changes to the repo locally on your machine.



Installing dependencies
See the README for guidance on installing the dependencies and getting started with development.


Adding or editing content
Each section is one directory under guidance, numbered so the order is visible, holding a single index.qmd. The directory name carries the number, so guidance/07-deciding-your-assurance-level/ is section 7. A section with more than one page keeps them beside its index.qmd, which is what the roles directory and the assurance level directory both do.
One directory is deliberately not numbered. guidance/analytical-cycle/ is the front page for the five phases rather than a section of its own, and a number on it would say it was a sixth phase.
Three things are named in one place each, and all three need updating together when a section is added or renamed. Miss one and the page still builds, so nothing tells you:

The three places that name a page






Item
Where




Whether the page is rendered at all
the render: list in _quarto.yml


Where it appears in the left sidebar
the sidebar: section of _quarto.yml


Where it appears in the Guidance menu
the navbar: section of _quarto.yml, which names the spine only, so a page can be correctly absent from it




To edit an existing page

Open the index.qmd in that section’s directory and edit it as markdown.
Text that belongs on more than one page lives in guidance/_partials/ and is pulled in with {{< include /guidance/_partials/name.qmd >}}. Edit the partial, not the copies. The include path starts from the project root, because a partial is included at more than one depth.
Once you are happy with your changes submit a pull request!



To add a new section

Create a subfolder within guidance, numbered so it sorts where you want it (e.g. 14-something-new).
Add an index.qmd to it with this header: ---  title: "The title of your page"  description: "One sentence saying what the page is for"  --- The title, the sidebar label and the navbar label should all say the same thing, so a reader arrives at the page they expected. The description is the browser meta description.
Add the content below the header using standard markdown syntax.
Add the page in all four places in the table above.
Render locally with quarto render and check the page appears in the sidebar, in the menu and in the contents table.
Once you are happy with your changes submit a pull request!



Before you open the pull request
Run the checks. They are quick and they assert things that are easy to break without noticing:
quarto render && bash checks/run-all.sh
That runs all of them. Several read the built site, so render first. If you only want the two that most often catch a new page, they are checks/accessibility.py and checks/links.py, and the first needs a render.

This statement applies to the Producing Quality Analysis Playbook. It does not cover the other NHSBSA sites and playbooks linked from it, which publish their own statements.

title: Accessibility
text:
This statement applies to the Producing Quality Analysis Playbook. It does not cover the other NHSBSA sites and playbooks linked from it, which publish their own statements.
We want as many people as possible to be able to use this playbook. It is built to meet the Web Content Accessibility Guidelines (WCAG) 2.2 at level AA, and meets several level AAA criteria as well.

title: Accessibility
text:
What we have done
The site is built from text, so its content is headings, paragraphs, lists, tables and links, not pictures of them. Each diagram is described in words.

Every page has a title, one main heading, and headings that never skip a level
A skip link is the first thing a keyboard reaches, and takes you to the page itself. The sidebar and the navigation bar show which page you are on in words and in shape, not in colour alone
Links say where they go. Source numbers link to a Sources list at the foot of the page, and nothing pops up over the text
Every table has a caption and a header row. Where a first column names each row, it is marked as row headers, so a screen reader can say which row a cell is in
On a phone a table of three or more columns is shown one row at a time, each cell under the name of its column, and is still announced as a table
The glossary has a filter box. It says how many entries match as you type
Text reflows to one column at 320 pixels wide, and at 400 percent zoom, without sideways scrolling. On a phone or a short window the bars stay in the page and are not pinned over it
On a phone the sidebar takes focus when it opens, gives it back when it closes, and puts the page behind it out of reach
Every control that takes keyboard focus shows a ring of two colours, so that it can be seen on a light or a dark ground
Each diagram has a text description under it, and opens on its own page as an SVG that scales to any zoom. On a narrow screen it scrolls sideways inside its own box, as WCAG 1.4.10 allows
Animation is switched off for anyone who has asked their device for less motion
Text and interface colours meet the required contrast, and nothing relies on colour alone

The playbook can also be built as a tagged PDF, an editable Word file and a tour of the site in photographs. These are alternative views of the web version, made on request, and they are not the published playbook. Each has a language, a title, an outline or heading styles, alternative text for every picture, and captions and header rows on every table.

title: Accessibility
section: What we have checked, and how
text:
What we have checked, and how
These claims are checked against the built pages every time the site is rebuilt. An accessibility engine tests every page against WCAG 2.0, 2.1 and 2.2 at levels A and AA, on a laptop, a phone and a phone at 400 percent zoom. Our own checks then test what an engine cannot see, such as where the skip link lands, whether Tab ever leaves a control off screen, and whether every focus ring can be seen, from a photograph of the screen.

title: Accessibility
section: Where we go beyond level AA
text:
Where we go beyond level AA
Four level AAA criteria are met and checked the same way.

The level AAA criteria the site meets, what each asks and what the site does







Criterion
What it asks
What the site does




1.4.6 Contrast (Enhanced)
7:1 for body text, 4.5:1 for large text
Links are NHS Dark Blue at 11.85:1, quiet text is NHS Dark Grey at 7.75:1, and white on the title banner clears 7:1


2.5.5 Target Size (Enhanced)
Anything you click or tap is at least 44 by 44 pixels
Navigation, footer, contents and card links, and the menu and sidebar buttons, are 44 pixels each way. A link in a sentence takes the exception for inline targets


2.4.9 Link Purpose (Link Only)
Every link makes sense on its own
No link reads “click here” or “read more”, or uses a web address as its text. Every link is checked on every build


2.4.10 Section Headings
Content is organised under headings
Every page of any length carries headings, so the on-this-page list is a usable route

title: Accessibility
section: Where we do not meet level AAA
text:
Where we do not meet level AAA
We do not claim level AAA for the whole site. The W3C advises against requiring it as a general policy, because some content cannot meet every AAA criterion. Two are out of reach for guidance of this kind, and a third is not claimed.
3.1.4 Expansion of short forms asks that the meaning of every short form is available. Most are spelled out where they first appear, and a few, such as ARIMA, are not.
3.1.5 Reading Level asks for text a person with lower secondary education can understand, or a simpler version. The Resource pages cite clause numbers from GovS 010 and the AQuA Book and use the vocabulary of analytical assurance, because their readers need the exact terms. The glossary in Resources is a partial answer.
1.4.8 Visual Presentation asks, among other things, for lines of no more than 80 characters. WCAG sets no limit on line length at level AA, which is the level the site meets here. The text column is set for reading, at about 67 characters on an ordinary line, and grows with the reader’s text size. Some lines are longer.

title: Accessibility
text:
What we have not tested
No screen reader, magnifier or speech input testing has been carried out against the published site, and none on a real phone or tablet. What has been tested is the markup and what a browser shows, by an accessibility engine, by our own measurements and by walking the keyboard through the site at several screen sizes. Automated checks find only the faults they are written to look for.
Some corrections, including the skip link and the names of the navigation landmarks, are made by a script when the page loads. With scripts switched off the pages still read in order, but those corrections are missing.
Parts of this site may still not be fully accessible, and this statement describes the work done rather than a tested result. If you find a problem, we want to hear about it.

title: The seven quality principles
text: NHSBSA analysis informs how public money is spent, how services are run, and what the public is told. Seven principles apply to all of it.

title: The seven quality principles
text:
The principles


1. Analysis answers the right questions


There should be a clear, shared understanding of the questions to be answered, how they meet user needs, and how certain the answer needs to be. Analysis should be for the public good and aligned to government policy and organisational objectives.




2. Using the right methods


Analysis uses appropriate inputs and methods to produce high quality results. It should be repeatable, independent, grounded in reality, objective, with uncertainty understood and managed, and it should answer the original question robustly.




3. At the right time


Analysis is provided in time to be useful. That is never at the expense of quality assurance.




4. With the right level of quality assurance


Quality assurance and continuous improvement are built into the way analysis is carried out. Assurance is proportionate to the impact of the results on the decision, and to the risks of how they will be used.




5. Following the right standards


Analysis is undertaken in line with legal and ethical obligations, with public service codes of conduct, and with those of your own profession.




6. Presented in the right way


Analysis supports effective decision-making and meets user needs through clearly presented, impartial, timely and accessible outputs. That includes being clear about context, strengths, limitations, and what remains uncertain, stated plainly enough to act on.




7. So the right decisions are made


Good quality analysis can be trusted to support effective decision-making and meet user needs.

title: Phase 2. Design
text:
Every level means all work. A mark such as From Level 2 means that level and above.

Every level: Choose the method. If the work is a model, find its type in the eight types of analytical model.
Every level: Score the likelihood, then read your level. Follow Step 2, score the likelihood and Step 3, read your level in the Analytical Assurance Decision Tool. Write the finished level into the Specification. If an impact dimension scored 4, go to Business Critical analysis.
Every level: Write the design and plan, and share it with everyone involved. The analysis plan template sets out what a plan covers. Also record:

whether the data sources are fit to answer the question
how somebody else running the method would get the same results
any ethics concern
any recommendation in a standard that you do not follow, and why
when the output will be reviewed

If time or resources limit the approach, tell your commissioner what risks follow.

Concepts and definitions






NoneConcepts and Definitions for Business-Critical Analysis










Business Critical Analysis
Informs major policy, funding, statutory, regulatory or customer-impacting decisions. The analysis is essential to the achievement of business plan actions and priorities. Errors could lead to significant patient or user impacts or serious financial, legal, reputational damages or penalties.


Assurance

title: Business-Critical Analysis
section: Deciding whether the analysis is business-critical
text:
Deciding whether the analysis is business-critical
It is the responsibility of the commissioner to determine whether the analysis is business critical.
When the scope has been completed, use the impact assessment in the Analytical Assurance Decision Tool to determine whether it meets the criteria for business-critical. The impact is assessed on a scale of 1 (low) to 4 (very high). Business Critical is defined by a level 4 score in any of these dimensions:

The extent to which the analysis influences decisions, actions, services or outcomes
The potential effect on expenditure, funding, resource allocation or financial performance
The potential effect on customer rights, entitlements, access, experience or outcomes
The potential effect on confidence in NHSBSA, its services or its analytical capability
The potential for regulatory breaches, legal challenge or non-compliance with statutory requirements
The extent to which the analysis is subject to external use, publication or public scrutiny

If the risk is scored as a four for at least one of the impact dimensions in the analytical risk assessment, then the analysis is designated as business-critical and the highest level of assurance is required. Publication status, Board consideration, Official Statistics designation, media interest, national visibility, FOI disclosure, ministerial interest or parliamentary scrutiny do not by themselves justify a Level 4 score.
The likelihood of an error does not change the business-critical classification.

title: R10. Data ethics and personal data
text: Analysis at NHSBSA uses data about people, and informs decisions that affect them. This page covers data ethics, personal data, and what to record when one of the ethics questions raises a concern.
crumbs: R10. Data ethics and personal data

title: R10. Data ethics and personal data
text:
Data ethics
Analysis should be undertaken in line with legal and ethical obligations and any other relevant public service codes of conduct.1
The Data and AI Ethics Framework provides guidance on using data appropriately and responsibly when planning, implementing and evaluating a policy or service.2

Use the Data and AI Ethics Framework, the current title
Government Functional Standard GovS 010: Analysis cites it as the Data Ethics Framework, which is the 2020 edition. On 18 December 2025 it was retitled the Data and AI Ethics Framework. Its scope was extended to AI and algorithmic technologies, and four principles were added. Use the current framework.
The framework includes a self-assessment tool. Use it instead of writing your own checklist.
Consider ethics when you design the work, not as a check at the end. The framework has seven principles. Ask each one as a question before the work starts.

Transparency. Could you explain to the people in the data what you did and why?
Accountability. Who is answerable if this turns out to be wrong?
Fairness. Could the analysis, or the decision it informs, affect some groups differently? Five questions make it answerable. Who is represented in the data, and in what proportion? Who is missing from it altogether? Is any variable acting as a proxy for a protected or sensitive characteristic? Do outcomes differ across groups once you look? How much fairness work is proportionate to what this analysis decides? An exploratory count at Level 1 does not need a bias audit. A model that decides who is eligible for something does.
Privacy. Do you use only the data the question requires? NHSBSA’s Statistical Disclosure Control protocol already answers this. NHSBSA templates and documents lists the protocol with the other NHSBSA documents this playbook draws on. Follow those documents directly.
Environmental sustainability. What does producing and running this analysis cost, and is that proportionate to what it is for? This matters most for repeated pipelines and for anything using large models.
Societal impact. Who is affected by the decision this analysis informs, beyond the people in the data? Ask it at scoping, in Phase 1, engagement and scoping.
Safety. What harm could follow if this is wrong, misread, or used for something it was not built for?

Raise societal impact and safety at scoping, while there is still time to act on the answer.
Answer the accountability question first. If nobody can answer it, the governance is not yet in place. See roles and responsibilities.


A gap in coverage is a fairness question
At Level 2, the checks by level include an understanding of the impacts of data quality. The input data is profiled for ranges, nulls, duplicates and outliers, and for what each means for the answer. That includes who is missing from it.
A gap in coverage is not only a wider interval. It is a blind spot in the conclusion, because the analysis cannot see the group that is missing. It is also a risk of affecting one group differently.
Uncertainty, assumptions and limitations covers the uncertainty side, where a gap in coverage limits what the figures can be used for.

title: R10. Data ethics and personal data
text:
When a question raises something
Where one of the seven questions raises a concern, record the concern and what you decided about it.
Record six things. Put them in a short block in the project record. They are the same six whether the concern is fairness, privacy, safety or societal impact.

The six fields to record for a concern, and what goes in each






Field
What goes in it




Affected groups
Who is affected by this, in the data and beyond it


Harms and benefits
What could go wrong, and what the analysis is for. Record both


Mitigations
What you actually changed: the method, the caveat, the scope, the publication decision


Residual risk
What is still there after the mitigations, stated plainly


Accountable decision-maker
The role that accepted that residual risk. The analyst only if they hold that authority


Escalation route
Where it went, if the analyst and the commissioner could not settle it between them



Record the six fields whether or not the concern was settled.

Escalating an ethical concern
A design and plan should cover escalation routes that let analysts and stakeholders raise concerns.3
Take it to the commissioner first, because they own the decision the analysis informs. This is the same route as in roles and responsibilities. If it is still not settled, take it to the Analytical Quality and Assurance Lead.
If the concern is about something that will be published as an official statistic, take it to the Lead Official for Statistics. That is already the route for whether an output is fit to publish.
Refusing to do a piece of analysis is a legitimate outcome of this route, and it is not the analyst’s alone to take. That is what the accountable decision-maker field is for.

title: R10. Data ethics and personal data
text:
Personal data
If you use personal data in analysis, you must use it in line with NHSBSA policy and prevailing legislation. GovS 010 says the same, as a recommendation: the use should be in accordance with the organisation’s policies and prevailing legislation.4
Where analysis using personal data is published, you may include in the publication:4

when personal data has been used, and the justification for its use
how guidance has been followed
the steps taken to protect the data

Information and data should be classified and securely managed in line with GovS 007 Security. They should also be retained to meet statutory and contractual requirements, and those of the Data and AI Ethics Framework.5
Ask before the work starts, not at sign-off. The information governance function provides information governance advice and owns the corporate data protection impact assessment (DPIA) process. Ask your team lead, or use the routes in who to ask, to start a DPIA.
Ask while you are still deciding what data to use. A DPIA raised after the analysis is built can only review a decision already taken.

text: Once you publish a figure, you cannot control how it is used. This page sets out what that asks of you, and where NHSBSA analysis is published.

title: R12. Publishing analysis
text:
Intelligent transparency
The Code of Practice for Statistics sets out intelligent transparency: taking an open, clear and accessible approach to the use of data, statistics and wider analysis in the public domain. Take this approach by default, every time.
It applies to more than official statistics. The Code’s Standards for the Public Use of Statistics, Data and Wider Analysis apply to public bodies using statistics, data and wider analysis in the public domain. They apply to everyone involved in that use, not to analysts alone. A figure quoted in a press release, a board paper made public, or a number given to a journalist is in scope. There are three standards.1
1. Equality of access. Make what is used in the public domain available to everyone in a timely way, so the public can access, scrutinise and verify the claims made from it.

draw on the latest and most reliable published official statistics where possible
publish the figures in advance of, or at the same time as, their use in public communications
publish them separately from any related policy or ministerial statement
if unpublished figures are referred to publicly, publish them as soon as possible, ideally the same day

2. Supporting understanding. Use figures with integrity and communicate them with clarity and accuracy, so the public can understand the basis for the claims made.

do not cherry-pick figures, take them out of context, or place undue certainty on them
communicate the key context and limitations alongside them
be clear where the figures came from, citing sources in publications and on social media
take proactive steps to prevent or minimise misinterpretation and misuse

3. Decision making and leadership. Seek and use impartial, expert advice when using figures in the public domain.

Quoting an unpublished figure in public commits you to publishing it
Under equality of access, publish a number quoted in public as soon as possible, ideally the same day. Until it is published, nobody can check the claim made from it.
If an analysis is going to be quoted before it is published, discuss this while the analysis is being scoped.

the code, published where it can be

title: R14. Why the level is scored as it is
text:
How the tool scores

Where the scales come from
The scales come from the NHSBSA Analytical Assurance Decision Tool, dated 13 October 2026. The impact scale covers the same ground as three of the AQuA Book factors: business criticality, relevance to the decision and effects on the public.1 NHSBSA has written its six impact dimensions in its own words.
Step 1, score the impact and Step 2, score the likelihood send you to the Analytical Assurance Decision Tool spreadsheet for the scales, so there is one version of them. You need an NHSBSA account with access to open it.


What each score measures
The impact score is about what an error would do, not about how hard the work is. The likelihood score is about how easily the analysis could be wrong.
Each dimension is scored against the tool’s description for each level, not against the dimension’s name. The methods the likelihood descriptions name are examples, not a complete list. The tool marks the finance thresholds as still to be confirmed, so use the figures in the version you open.


The highest score decides the level
The highest single score decides the level, and scores are not averaged. This is the playbook’s own rule, and no standard states it. Three reasons support it.

One high-risk answer is enough, because that risk is real however routine the rest of the work is.
Over-assuring one piece of analysis costs a few hours. Under-assuring a Business Critical one can cost far more. For the same reason, take the higher level where two answers both look defensible.
Averaging can leave a patient-facing output at Level 1 Standard, for example one produced by an experienced team from one clean data source. This is an illustration, not an NHSBSA case.



Recording each score when you make it
Record each score when you make it. The reasons are the playbook’s own.

The level is finished while it can still shape the method.
A level recorded after the work is done only describes what was done. It cannot be explained to somebody six months later.
The level has to be settled before the assurance is planned, because a level agreed after the method is fixed cannot change the method.



Scoring again
A score stays valid while the work it describes stays the same. Score again sooner than Phase 5, review if the data, the method, the audience or the decision the work informs changes, and record why.
Before work is reused for a new purpose, the four checks before reuse decide whether it is scored again. Reuse and the assurance level explains why.
An output that runs to a schedule is scored once, when it is designed, and not on every run. A one-off that has become a regular production run is a different piece of work, and is scored again rather than inheriting the one-off’s level. Both rules are the playbook’s own.


Scoring the likelihood once the method is chosen
The likelihood is scored at design, once the data and the method are settled. All six dimensions ask about the chosen approach, so you cannot score them until it is chosen.
Likelihood depends on:

how complex the data and the analysis are
how much rests on assumptions
how novel the approach is
how much is done by hand
how well it is documented

Business Critical work is the exception: see why a full likelihood check is not required.


The three prompts
The three prompts catch work where the score alone does not show the whole risk. They take little time to answer while the tool is open. None of them raises the level by itself.
The prompt on repeated decisions has its own reason. A one-off relies on its assumptions once. A repeating output relies on them every time it runs, until somebody checks them.


Scoring the level instead of judging it
The level is scored rather than judged. Assurance is proportionate to the work.2 The AQuA Book lists what makes a piece of analysis need more of it.1
The playbook uses a shorter list of seven factors:

the risks of its intended use
its type and complexity
the novelty of the approach
the importance of the issue
how central it is to the decision
the precision required
the resource available

These seven are the playbook’s own list. Table 3-1 in AQuA Book section 3.1 gives ten factors in different words, including the reuse of existing work, the longevity of the analysis, effects on the public and repeat runs of the same analysis.1
Scoring that list is how two people reach the same answer independently. It is also how the answer can be looked up six months later.


The eight model types
The list of eight types of analytical model is NHSBSA’s own. You place a model among the eight types after you have your level. For models used in decision making, GovS 010 section 6.11 says they should be robust and fit for purpose.3

The eight model types and what each is for






Type
What it is for




Policy simulation
To better understand the options that drive a decision. It estimates the likely cost and impact of each choice before it is made


Forecasting
To predict the future and inform today’s choices. Projections of demand, volume or cost that let future pressures be understood while there is still time to act


Financial evaluation
To better understand future liabilities or costs, where a commitment made now is paid for over many years


Procurement and commercial evaluation
For the letting and management of large contracts, and to ensure value for money


Planning
To make workforce and capacity decisions which affect the delivery of future services


Science based
To better understand and simulate the physical environment, in order to evaluate possible solutions or to mitigate potentially damaging impacts


Allocation of funds
To determine how funds are distributed, so that they are allocated properly against need and underpin local service delivery


Conceptual
To help understand the key influences that are important to a system being modelled



The type is not a seventh impact dimension, and it is not scored. It works as a check on the six impact scores. A model that allocates funds and a model that structures a concept carry very different consequences when they are wrong.
A model can be Business Critical whatever its type. The impact it carries decides that, not where it sits in the list.
Conceptual models are developed with a range of problem-structuring techniques.

title: R14. Why the level is scored as it is
section: Reading and working to your level
text:
Reading and working to your level

What Level 1 means
Level 1 Standard is not “no assurance”. Someone separate from the analyst, within the team, still checks the headline numbers. Each level includes the checks of the levels below it shows how independent the assurer is from the analyst at each level.


Each level includes the checks of the levels below it
Levels are cumulative: each level includes everything the levels below it require. Level 3 includes the requirements of Levels 1 and 2, and Level 4 BCA includes all three.
The independence of the assurer shows how each level adds to the one below.

Level 1 Standard: a colleague within the team checks the headline numbers.
Level 2 Enhanced: review by someone who was not involved in producing the work.
Level 3 Comprehensive: assurance from outside the team and publication of the quality assurance statement.
Level 4 BCA: a Lead Assurer from outside the delivering team, with external review.

An older NHSBSA document may say Tier where the playbook says Level. They map one for one: Tier 3 is Level 3 Comprehensive. The word changed because the older word named one set of activities on its own, while a Level includes everything the levels below it require.


Where the checks by level come from
The names of the checks in the table on Step 4, what your level requires are NHSBSA’s own. They come from the section “Required checks in each level” of the Analytical Assurance Decision Tool, which lists the names only. The “What that means here” column is this playbook’s reading of each check.
The tool lists 29 checks. Seven are first required at Level 1, nine at Level 2, eight at Level 3 and five at Level 4 BCA. Additional scenario testing appears at both Level 3 and Level 4.


Working to a deadline
The assurance level is set by what the work needs, not by how much time there is. AQuA Book chapter 3 says assurance should be proportionate to the potential effect of the analysis and to its size and complexity.2
The tool expects assurance to be done under time pressure, not skipped. Level 1 checks are for low risk analyses “and when there is very limited time to carry out assurance”. Both Level 2 and Level 3 carry “and for analyses with very limited time, if time permits”.
The same clause on two levels is not an order to drop to a lower level. Where there is little time for review or for putting issues right, the tool’s working-at-pace row says to carry out the Level 1 activities and add further checks where time permits. It also says to document any omitted activities and to communicate the residual risks to decision makers. The level stands, and the assurance is fitted to the time available.
To meet a deadline, narrow the question rather than lowering the assurance level. A narrower question answered properly is more useful than a broad one answered unreliably, and it is usually possible. Where it is not, say plainly what assurance was not done.
AQuA Book section 3.2 says that where time and resource constraints make full assurance impossible, addressing the areas of greatest risk should take priority. It says the analyst should tell the commissioner how the risks were addressed, what risks remain and the caveats.4 Section 4.2.1 says that where time constraints mean insufficient assurance has taken place, this should be explicitly acknowledged and reported in an assurance statement that sets out the known limitations and conditions.5
Record the level the work needs, not a lower one. A lower level would hide that the skipped assurance was ever needed.
Assurance takes time and resource. The commissioner is responsible for making sure there is enough of both, not the analyst.
A disagreement about the level goes to the Analytical Quality and Assurance Lead, as where each disagreement goes sets out.
