title: R16. Why the roles work as they do
text:
The critical friend and independence

Independence at every level
At every level, someone independent looks at the work, and the analyst does their own checks. The analyst’s own checks come first, and nobody else’s review replaces them.
The AQuA Book says the assurer and the analyst shall be independent. This does not stop the analyst undertaking assurance, but there shall also be some formal independent assurance.1 Responsibility for formal assurance to the approver and the commissioner lies with the assurer. The analyst should carry out their own assurance.2
Each level includes the checks of the levels below it shows how the levels build on one another.


Where assurance comes from
Beyond one assignment, GovS 010 says assurance should typically come from at least three separate and defined places.3 These are operational management, senior management independent of it, and independent bodies.
GovS 010 also says analysis should be peer reviewed by independent individuals or groups.4 It says “should”, so this is a recommendation.


What the critical friend confirms
GovS 010 has the analytical assurer give independent advice on the assignment and, in particular, confirm that quality assurance has taken place and that the use of the outputs, the assumptions and the risks are understood.5 The playbook asks the critical friend to confirm these three things. This is narrower than a general opinion of the work.

That appropriate and sufficient analytical quality assurance has taken place. The playbook measures this against the assurance level.
That the use of the outputs is appropriate. In the playbook, this means the results can support the decision they will be used for.
That assumptions and risks are understood.

The critical friend gives advice.5 The commissioner owns the decision, and the analyst owns the analysis.


Naming and working with the critical friend
A critical friend named before the work starts can shape the plan and put their own time in the schedule. One found afterwards can only check the result. This fits GovS 010, which says the analytical assurer should check that the proposed design meets the commissioner’s requirements.6
Look for someone with experience of similar data or techniques. If the analyst is the area expert, they can consider a newer colleague instead. The newer colleague gains the experience, and the analyst’s work is read by somebody who does not share the analyst’s assumptions.
Ask the team lead first, as who to ask says. The Data Science team or the Data Science Lead can recommend someone.
To involve the critical friend throughout the work, not only at the end:

meet regularly
review in small increments
plan their time into the schedule
give notice when a review is needed

title: R16. Why the roles work as they do
section: The Analysis Senior Responsible Officer’s accountability
text:
The Analysis Senior Responsible Officer’s accountability

Naming the Analysis Senior Responsible Officer at scoping
The Analysis Senior Responsible Officer is named at scoping, not at sign-off. The commissioner names them, with the Analytical Quality and Assurance Lead. Naming the officer only when the work is designed, and someone notices a signature is needed, is too late, because most of the lifecycle will already have happened.
The register entry is made at the same time. Naming the officer at scoping is the playbook’s own judgement.


What the Analysis Senior Responsible Officer confirms
The officer confirms that the work is suitable for its intended use. That is a judgement about fitness for a purpose, made on the assurance evidence in front of the officer.
The AQuA Book calls this role the approver, who shall review the assurance evidence provided to them.7 GovS 010 asks for confirmation from the accountable officer that a recommended practice model is suitable for its intended use.8
It is not a second technical review. That is the playbook’s reading of the role. The Lead Assurer has done the technical review and reports to the officer, and the AQuA Book has the assurer review the assurance completed by the analyst.9 The AQuA Book also has the approver scrutinise the work of the analyst and the assurer.2
At Level 4 BCA the Lead Assurer signs off first, then the officer.


When the officer is also the commissioner
The officer and the commissioner can be the same person, in which case both sets of responsibilities apply. The independence the assurance level requires is unaffected. It applies between the assurer and the analyst, not between the officer and either of them.
The AQuA Book says the assurer and the analyst shall be independent1 and that their roles shall be separate from one another in all cases.2

title: R16. Why the roles work as they do
text:
The commissioner and the analyst

Start from the decision
The commissioner states the decision the analysis informs, not the output they want. That makes the conversation about scope a short one. Scoping defines the problem and aligns expectations with what can be delivered.10
GovS 010 lists ensuring that the brief is defined and clearly communicated among the commissioner’s activities.11 It has the analyst assist the commissioner in structuring the question, to ensure the right analysis is performed.12
Challenging a brief is therefore part of the analyst’s job. The analyst can be expected to challenge a request that arrives already framed as an output.


Draft results go to the commissioner first
In Phase 4, delivery, communication and sign-off, the analyst hands the draft results to the commissioner first. The commissioner then understands the analysis before approving it and before sign-off.
GovS 010 gives the same reason: draft results should be delivered to the commissioner to ensure they are sufficiently understood prior to approval.13 The AQuA Book has insights and assurances communicated to the approver and the commissioner, and says they should understand them well enough to decide whether the work has been appropriately assured and meets their requirements.14


Passing results on with their caveats
If a result is passed on without its caveats, the person receiving it cannot see its limits. GovS 010 asks for caveats so that results are used appropriately.15 The AQuA Book asks the commissioner to understand and apply any limitations.16


Who counts as a commissioner
Commissioners are the people who request analysis, including non-analysts and third-party suppliers. A commissioner may be an internal team, an external partner, or a sponsor such as the Department of Health and Social Care or NHS England.

title: R16. Why the roles work as they do
text:
Disagreements and the organisation

Where each disagreement goes
The reasons for three of the routes in where a disagreement goes are these.

The assurance level goes to the Analytical Quality and Assurance Lead. The level is the one decision that is neither the commissioner’s nor the analyst’s alone.
An ethical concern goes to the commissioner first, because they own the decision the analysis informs.
Whether there is enough time for the assurance goes to the commissioner first, because ensuring there is enough time and resource is a commissioner responsibility.

Four of the five routes end at the same person, the Analytical Quality and Assurance Lead.
See working to a deadline for the reasoning on time and resource. See escalating an ethical concern for the rest of that route.


Cover for the Analytical Quality and Assurance Lead
There is no appointed deputy for the Analytical Quality and Assurance Lead, and no agreed time by which a level dispute is answered.
If the post holder is unavailable, the person raising the dispute takes it through their own line while they wait, rather than letting the work stall. Where a disagreement goes gives that step.


The roles in the standards
The standards call the critical friend the analytical assurer. GovS 010 defines the role at section 4.4.6,5 and the AQuA Book defines it, as the assurer, at section 5.1.2
The same role under another name lists the other names the roles go under. What is binding covers what GovS 010 asks of NHSBSA for the senior officer accountable for analysis and the defined roles.

text:
An illustration at Level 4

A funding allocation formula through the four roles
Illustrative example, not a real NHSBSA case. This is what the playbook asks of work of that kind.
NHSBSA’s Analytical Assurance Decision Tool gives a funding allocation formula as a worked example of impact 4. This example follows the formula through all four roles, so you can read the guidance for each role against one piece of work.

Commissioner
The playbook asks the commissioner to:

state the decision the formula informs, the deadline, and how certain the answer has to be. See Phase 1, engagement and scoping.
score the six impact dimensions with the analyst. One dimension at 4 makes the work Business Critical. See Deciding your assurance level (the Analytical Assurance Decision Tool).

The Finance row scores 4 for analysis that “determines, or is relied on for, major funding, investment, commissioning, resource-allocation or policy decisions”. A funding allocation formula is that kind of analysis, so the work is Business Critical, at Level 4 BCA.
The playbook then asks the commissioner to say so at scoping, before the design. It also asks the commissioner to find the time and resource Level 4 assurance needs, or agree a narrower question.


Analyst
The playbook asks the analyst to:

agree the question, and record the scope, the boundaries and the assumptions. See Phase 1, engagement and scoping.
score the impact with the commissioner, and read Level 4 BCA off the Analytical Assurance Decision Tool at scoping.
choose the method, and place it among the eight model types. See Phase 2, design.
do their own verification and validation first.
log decisions as they make them.
quantify the uncertainty, and say what rests on which assumption. See Uncertainty, assumptions and limitations.



Critical friend
At Level 4 the critical friend is a Lead Assurer from outside the delivering team. External review applies as well. How independent you have to be covers this.
The playbook asks the critical friend to:

be named at design.
reproduce the calculations from source.
review the documentation itself, not only the numbers.
examine the structural and conceptual assumptions, and report what they find back.



Analysis Senior Responsible Officer
The Analysis Senior Responsible Officer is named at scoping, and the register entry is made then. See Business Critical analysis.
The playbook asks the Analysis Senior Responsible Officer to:

confirm design governance has been followed before the analysis starts.
review the assurance evidence, and approve the formula as fit for its intended use, after the Lead Assurer has signed off.
revalidate the designation annually, and before any reuse for a new purpose. See Phase 5, review.

title: R18. Worked examples
text:
Example impacts and assurance levels

Where the example impacts come from
The impact examples in the second column of Find your kind of work are NHSBSA’s. They come from the annex of worked examples to the Analytical Assurance Decision Tool. NHSBSA marks the tool’s annex as still to be developed, and the annex is undated.
A Parliamentary Question is the playbook’s addition, not one of NHSBSA’s worked examples.
Your assurance level is where that impact meets your likelihood, so at impact 1 to 3 it can be lower than the highest level for that impact. At impact 4 it is Level 4 BCA at every likelihood.


One impact score, two levels
Two pieces of work on the same impact row can reach different levels if their likelihood differs. On the impact 3 row of the matrix, likelihood 1 gives Level 1 Standard and likelihood 3 gives Level 3 Comprehensive.
These two illustrations are not NHSBSA cases.

A Freedom of Information (FOI) response built from one clean dataset by an established method scores Level 1 on likelihood. At impact 3 that is Level 1 Standard on the matrix. The same response would be Level 3 Comprehensive if its likelihood scored 3.
Exploratory analysis built by hand on a novel method scores Level 4 on likelihood. At impact 1 that is only Level 2 Enhanced on the matrix, because the impact score sets the row.

Where the principles come from
Five of the seven are GovS 010’s own (GovS 010 section 2), so following them is how NHSBSA meets the standard rather than something extra on top. The third and the seventh are NHSBSA’s.

Which parts of GovS 010 are a requirement, and which are a recommendation
GovS 010 separates shall, a requirement, from should, a recommendation. Only three of its requirements are substantive:

the principles, which the standard puts as “those engaged in analysis shall ensure” (GovS 010 section 2)
a senior officer accountable for NHSBSA’s analysis activities

The count of shall, the clauses and the meaning of should are in what is binding.

title: R19. Standards to principles mapping
section: What each principle means in practice
text:
What each principle means in practice

1. Analysis answers the right questions
An analysis with no agreed margin of error has no threshold to be tested against. Agree it at scoping, record it in the analytical plan, design against it, and say at the end what is still uncertain. Uncertainty, assumptions and limitations is how you measure it, and Phase 1, engagement and scoping is where you agree it.

Why this sits in the principles rather than in a method
Three sources ask for the agreement rather than the measurement. GovS 010 asks for the levels of quality and certainty required to be agreed and recorded at scoping (GovS 010 section 5.2). At design, the AQuA Book asks analysts to search the planned analysis for sources of uncertainty large enough to breach “the acceptable margin of error”. Somebody has to have said what that margin is (AQuA Book section 7.4). And the Uncertainty Toolkit for Analysts gives its whole second chapter to jointly agreeing how uncertainty should be used, before the analysis is designed. None of the three is about measuring uncertainty. They are about agreeing how much uncertainty the decision can accept, while there is still time to design for it.



2. Using the right methods
Repeatable, independent, grounded in reality, objective, with uncertainty understood and managed, and answering the original question robustly: that is RIGOUR, set out in full in what each standard asks for.


3. At the right time
Where time is short, narrow the question and answer it properly.


4. With the right level of quality assurance
What a review finds goes into the next piece of work.

title: R19. Standards to principles mapping
section: What goes wrong when quality is assumed
text:
What goes wrong when quality is assumed
Poor analytical quality is rarely obvious at the time. Four patterns are common, and each is a process failure rather than a competence failure.
A figure is quoted without its caveat. The figure appears in a paper. The caveat that qualified it sat in an annex and was not included in the paper. A decision is taken on a number that meant something narrower than the reader thought.
A one-off becomes a production run. Work built quickly for a single question turns out to be useful and is rerun for months. Nobody re-assesses anything, because no single moment felt like a decision.
Assurance is done but not recorded. Somebody checked. Nobody can now say what they checked, when, or what they found. The work cannot be defended, and a practice area cannot be evidenced as compliant.
Effort goes to the wrong place. Low-risk work is over-engineered because that is the only standard anyone has set out. High-risk work is assured thinly because the deadline was short.
Each is what the practices in this playbook are there to catch.

title: R19. Standards to principles mapping
text:
Where this playbook answers GovS 010
Three things have to be true of every piece of analysis. The quality and certainty required is agreed and recorded. The checks that deliver it are proportionate to the risk. And somebody is accountable for the analysis.
Deciding your assurance level, the checks, by level and roles and responsibilities are where the playbook does each of them.

title: R6. Correcting a published figure
text: An error can still reach publication. What you do next decides whether it damages trust. For official statistics, NHSBSA’s policy sets out what to do.

title: R6. Correcting a published figure
section: What to do when a published figure has changed
text:
What to do when a published figure has changed
The NHSBSA Revisions and Corrections Policy (PDF) treats a revision and a correction as two different things. A revision is expected: statistics published as provisional and later finalised, a change of methodology, or the arrival of further data. A correction is an error.



When a published figure has changed. Select the diagram to open it on its own page, where you can zoom in. Scroll sideways to see all of it.




Text description of this diagram


A gold question at the top left asks: was the change expected? An arrow marked yes goes right to a green box: a revision, which is expected and is not an error. An arrow marked no goes down to a wide blue box: a correction, which is an error, graded by what it does to the conclusions already drawn. Three arrows go down from it, one to each grade.

The three grades of error, and what happens for each






The error
What happens




Significant, where the change would contradict the conclusions previously drawn from the data
A prominent alert on the website, corrected as soon as possible, and communicated to users and stakeholders


Minor but significant, insubstantial but warranting immediate correction in professional judgement
The published release is amended and the revision is clearly identified in it


Minor but insignificant, where a correction would reasonably be deemed inconsequential
Corrected at the next scheduled release rather than immediately





The policy grades errors by what they do to the conclusions, not by how big the number is. For example, a small arithmetic slip that reverses a conclusion is significant. A large number restated without changing anything anyone decided is not significant.
The amendment is published alongside the link to the document. Where an error is known but corrected figures are not yet available, a note goes on the statistics saying so, and making clear the figures are subject to change.

Who decides
The policy names two deciders, in two of its parts.

An error in published statistics. The Lead Official for Statistics decides how to address it, consulting the National Statistician where appropriate. This is in the policy’s part on corrections.
Any change to published statistics. The statistician responsible for the publication decides, consulting the Lead Official for Statistics as appropriate. This is in its part on handling revisions and corrections.

The policy does not say which part governs when a correction is also a change, so involve both: the statistician responsible for the publication, and the Lead Official for Statistics. The part on handling revisions and corrections commits to telling the Lead Official of any significant revision or correction in any case. The governance and management framework records who holds that post. See who to ask for how to reach them.


For any other output
The policy does not bind other outputs, but its approach is good practice for any output. Say what was wrong, say what it changed, and say where the corrected version is. Leave the original visible rather than replacing it silently.

title: R8. What each standard asks for
text:
GovS 010: Analysis
The government functional standard for analysis. It sets out five principles and the governance and accountabilities for analysis in an organisation. It also covers the analytical cycle, which it sets out in five stages, and thirteen supporting practices. This playbook sets the same cycle out as five phases. Delivery, communication and sign-off are one phase, and review is added as the fifth.
The thirteen are: public interest; inputs and methods; supporting decision-making; uncertainty; analytical verification and validation; documentation and record keeping; quality assurance; collaborative working; learning from experience; analytical models; statistics; appraisal and evaluation; and personal data.1 Each has a section of this playbook that meets it, and where each standard is met says which.
When it applies: always. It applies to all analysis undertaken in government, whoever does it.
NHSBSA is assessed against GovS 010, and this playbook is part of how NHSBSA meets it.

What is binding
GovS 010 separates shall, a requirement, from should, a recommendation. Shall appears eleven times in the whole document. One of the eleven is in the conventions table that defines the term.
Seven of the remaining ten say that a different functional standard shall be followed: GovS 005 Digital, GovS 008 Commercial or GovS 011 Communication. That leaves three substantive requirements:

The principles. The standard puts them as “those engaged in analysis shall ensure”.2 Five of the seven principles in this playbook are the standard’s own, and R19. Standards to principles mapping names the clause each one answers to.
A senior officer accountable for analysis. GovS 010 requires NHSBSA to have a senior officer accountable for analysis as an activity.3
Analytical roles and accountabilities. GovS 010 requires NHSBSA to define analytical roles in its governance and management framework, and to assign them to people who can hold them.4 The standard describes those people as having appropriate seniority, skills and experience.

The first applies to the analyst. The other two apply to the organisation, separately from the four roles you hold on a piece of work.
NHSBSA records who holds the other two in its governance and management framework, not in this playbook.
Everything else in the standard is a should, the thirteen practices included. GovS 010 calls a should advisory. The AQuA Book adds that a should is met on a “comply or explain” basis,5 so you can depart from a should only with a reason you can explain. Record any departure and its reason.
The sentence “All analysis shall be assured” is not from GovS 010. It comes from chapter 3 of the AQuA Book.6 The Analytical Assurance Decision Tool states it as an instruction.

title: R8. What each standard asks for
text:
The AQuA Book
Guidance on producing quality analysis for government. Where GovS 010 sets the requirement, the AQuA Book says how to meet it.
Where the AQuA Book and GovS 010 overlap, the playbook follows the AQuA Book. That rule is the playbook’s own.
Four things in this playbook come from it. The analytical lifecycle, which the AQuA Book sets out in four stages.7 The proportionality approach in deciding your assurance level, which is its chapter 3.6 Its four roles, which are the four in roles and responsibilities.8 And the RIGOUR principles.9
Chapter 3 also states two requirements. All analysis shall be assured, and the assurer and the analyst shall be independent.6 The AQuA Book states further requirements with shall for the assurer, the approver and the analyst, in sections 5.1,8 8.1.3,10 9.1.211 and 9.1.4.12
When it applies: always, as the practical companion to GovS 010.

Quality assurance and engagement in every phase
The AQuA Book says that quality assurance activities should take place throughout an analytical project.7 It also says that an effective quality assurance process involves ongoing engagement between the commissioner and the analyst.
The engagement is there to keep an appropriate balance between time, resource and quality. It is also there to build a shared understanding of the assurance activities required and the risks involved.
In this playbook, quality assurance is:

planned in Phase 1, engagement and scoping
designed in Phase 2, design
done in Phase 3, analysis
stated in Phase 4, delivery, communication and sign-off
tested in Phase 5, review

Customer and stakeholder engagement runs through all five phases in the same way. The commissioner has a part in every phase.

title: R8. What each standard asks for
text:
RIGOUR, in full
Repeatable. For an analytical process to be considered valid we might reasonably expect that the analysis produces the same outputs for the same inputs and constraints. Different analysts might approach the analytical problem in different ways, while methods might include randomised processes. In such cases, exact matches are not guaranteed or expected. Taking this into account, repeatability means that if an approach is repeated the results should be as expected.
Independent. Analysis should be (as far as possible) free of prejudice or bias. Care should be taken to balance views appropriately across all stakeholders and experts.
Grounded in reality. Quality analysis takes the Commissioner and Analyst on a journey as views and perceptions are challenged and connections are made between the analysis and its real consequences. Connecting with reality like this guards against failing to properly grasp the context of the problem that is being analysed.
Objective. Effective engagement and suitable challenge reduce the risk of bias and enables the Commissioner and the Analyst to be clear about the interpretation of results.
Uncertainty-managed. Uncertainty is identified, managed and communicated throughout the analytical process.
Robust. Analytical results are error free in the context of residual uncertainty and accepted limitations that make sure the analysis is used appropriately.9
Repeatable is not the same as automated. Reproducible and automated analysis compared sets out the difference.

Reproducible and automated analysis compared
Repeatable is the first letter of RIGOUR.9 It does not mean automated. Automation can help make analysis reproducible, but it is not enough on its own.
Reproducible and automated analysis both aim at efficiency and reliability. They work on different parts of the process. Each has its own question:

Reproducibility. Can someone else, or even you later on, given the same inputs, understand and recreate your work?
Automation. Can a computer run the analysis, with any valid inputs, with minimal or no human intervention?

Good practice is a fully reproducible analysis that includes a level of automation appropriate to the complexity and the effort of repeating it manually.
The two differ on six considerations.

Reproducible and automated analysis side by side, one consideration to a row







Consideration
Reproducible analysis
Automated analysis




Primary goal
Verifiability, transparency, reusability
Efficiency, scalability, speed


Main activities
Documenting all steps and key decisions, managing versions
Scripting, scheduling, pipelines, monitoring


Does it require automation?
No
Yes


Is it essential?
Yes
No, but desirable, especially as an analysis grows in complexity


Testing the analysis
Use static input data, for known results
Include tests that run automatically when the analysis changes


Consistency
In results
In processes

section: The Code of Practice for Statistics
text:
The Code of Practice for Statistics
Maintained by the UK Statistics Authority and regulated by the Office for Statistics Regulation. Edition 3.0 has been in force since 30 October 2025.
It keeps the three pillars of Trustworthiness, Quality and Value, and sets out ten Standards for Official Statistics beneath them.

Code of Practice for Statistics standards, their pillars and what producers must do







Standard
Pillar
Producers must




1. Show integrity
Trustworthiness
Act honestly, objectively and professionally, and challenge misuse


2. Lead responsibly
Trustworthiness
Make impartial decisions under the Head of Profession for Statistics


3. Be transparent
Trustworthiness
Release at a standard time, pre-announced


4. Manage data responsibly
Trustworthiness
Handle data safely and be open about its use


5. Prioritise quality
Quality
Support a quality culture that encourages learning and improvement


6. Be rigorous
Quality
Use suitable data and sound methods, and assure quality across production and release


7. Be open about quality
Quality
Explain strengths, limitations and uncertainty prominently


8. Be relevant
Value
Put users at the centre of decisions about the statistics


9. Be clear
Value
Present statistics to support appropriate interpretation


10. Be accessible
Value
Ensure statistics are accessible and freely available to all



When it applies: for official statistics, in full and as a regulatory requirement. NHSBSA official statistics are listed in the statistical collections.

You may apply the Code voluntarily
If you produce data, statistics or analysis that is not official statistics, you may still apply the Code to show a commitment to trustworthiness, quality and public value.13
Consider it for anything published or quoted externally. It is a choice, not an obligation, so make that choice deliberately.
Where each standard is met says which part of the playbook covers each of the ten Standards.
